INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGY IN INDIAN COURTS 
†2273. SHRI AJAY BHATT: 
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) the status of incorporation of information and communication technology in Indian 
Courts; 
(b) whether e-filing has been started in all the courts in the country including Uttarakhand; 
(c) if so, the details including Uttarakhand High Court and the present status thereof and the 
number of cases registered through the said e-filing method, court-wise; and 
(d) the steps taken or proposed to be taken by the Government to create awareness about the 
e-filing fund across the country? 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE (INDEPENDENT CHARGE) OF THE MINISTRY OF LAW 
AND JUSTICE; AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARJUN RAM MEGHWAL) 
(a): The e-Courts Mission Mode Project is being implemented in a phased manner across the 
country with the objective of strengthening the use of Information and Communication 
Technology (ICT) in the judicial system. Various ICT-enabled initiatives, including the Case 
Information System (CIS) 4.0, e -Filing, e Payments, Video Conferencing, Virtual Courts, 
Digital Case Records, National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG), Interoperable Criminal Justice 
System (ICJS), eSewa Kendras, National Service and Tracking of Electroni c Processes 
(NSTEP), the eCourts Services Portal and Mobile App, and other citizen -centric digital 
services, have been implemented across the High Courts and District Courts in a phased 
manner. 
(b): The e -Filing system is an end -to-end digital platform for the online filing of cases, 
written statements, replies and other related applications. As on 30.06.2026, the Rules for e-
Filing have been implemented in 25 High Courts, including the High Court of Uttarakhand 

2 
 
and the District Courts under its jurisdiction. As on 30.06.2026, a total of 1 .25 crore cases 
have been filed through the e -Filing system across the country. The details of cases filed 
through the e-Filing system, High Court-wise and District-wise, is placed at Annexure-I. 
(c): In the State of  Uttarakhand, a total of 1 .17 lakh cases have been filed through the e - 
Filing system before District Courts, including 356 cases efiled before the High Court of 
Uttarakhand. The District-wise details of cases filed through the e -Filing system in 
Uttarakhand, as received from the High Court of Uttarakhand, is placed at Annexure-II. 
(d): To create awareness and promote adoption of the e-Filing system across the country, the 
eCommittee, Supreme Court of India, in coordination with the High Courts, has undertaken 
training programmes, capacity -building workshops and orientation sessions for Judi cial 
Officers, court staff, advocates and other stakeholders through the State Judicial Academies 
and the respective High Courts. User manuals, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), FAQs 
and video tutorials have also been prepared and disseminated to facilitate effective use of the 
e-Filing system.  
Further, eSewa Kendras have been established across the country  to assist litigants and 
advocates in registration on the e -Filing portal, scanning and uploading of petitions and 
supporting documents, online payment of court fees and availing other services relating to e-
Filing, thereby promoting awareness and facilitating wider adoption of the e-Filing system.

entries.t: Ayushman Arogya Mandirs in Andhra Pradesh
entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
LOK SABHA
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 2274
TO BE ANSWERED ON 31st JULY,2026
AYUSHMANAROGYAMANDIRs IN ANDHRA PRADESH
2274. DR. C M RAMESH:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is true that the Government has approved 1800 units of Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
(Sub-Centres, Health and Wellness Centres) in Andhra Pradesh;
(b) if so, the details of AAMs approved, district-wise;
(c) the details of the amount of funds approved, sanctioned, released and spent on the above 1800
units in the said State, especially Anakapalli district;
(d) the timeframe by which the above AAMs are likely to become operational; and
(e) whether these AAMs are likely to provide comprehensive primary healthcare services
including non-communicable disease screening, teleconsultation, essential drugs & diagnostics
and wellness activities through these centres, if so, the details thereof?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (e): Public Health is a State subject. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare provides
technical and financial support to the States/UTs to strengthen the public healthcare services,
based on the proposals received in the form of Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) under
National Health Mission (NHM). Government of India provides approval for the proposals in the
form of Record of Proceedings (RoPs) as per norms & available resources.
As reported by States/UTs on Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM) portal, a total of 1,86,298
AAMs including 11873 AAMs in Andhra Pradesh have been operationalized by strengthening
Sub-health Centres (SHCs) and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) in the country, as on 30.06.2026.
District-wise number of AAMs operationalized in Andhra Pradesh is enclosed as Annexure.

The AAMs incrementally provide 12 package of primary health care services across the country,
encompassing Reproductive and child care services, Communicable diseases, Non Communicable
diseases (NCD), Palliative Care and elderly Care, Care for common mental disorders, neurological
conditions (epilepsy,dementia) and substance use disorders management (tobacco, alcohol, drugs),
Oral health, ENT care, and Basic emergency care. To complement the expanded services, the
essential list of drugs & diagnostics has been expanded to make 179 drugs & 63 diagnostics at PHC
-AAMs and 113 drugs & 14 diagnostics at SHC-AAMs in the country.
Details of State PIP approvals for the state of Andhra Pradesh for AAM under NHM during last
three years are as follows:

country. PM-ABHIM aims to support for infrastructure development for Building less SHC -
AAMs, Urban AAMs, Support for Block Public Health Units (BPHUs), Integrated Public Health

crore.

LOK SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 2275  
ANSWERED ON 31.07.2026  
  
SERVICE CONDITIONS OF AWWS  
  
2275. SHRI N K PREMACHANDRAN:  
 
 Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:  
 
(a)  whether the Union Government propose to increase the wages/honorarium and improve 
the service conditions of the Anganwadi Workers (AWWs), if so, the details thereof and 
action taken thereon; 
(b)  whether the Government proposes to restore the TA of the AWWs to attend the various 
programmes as part of their official duty, if so, the details thereof;  
(c)  whether the Union Government is considering the request of Kerala for restoration of TA, 
if  so, the details thereof; 
(d)  whether the Union Government proposes to release the increased honorarium of the 
AWWs as approved by APIP 2025 -2026, if so, the details thereof; and 
(e)  whether the Union Government proposes to provide ESIC benefits to the AWWs, if so, 
the details thereof? 
  
ANSWER 
  
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT  
(SHRIMATI SAVITRI THAKUR)  
(a) to (e) Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) and Anganwadi Helpers (AWHs) are honorary workers 
drawn from the local community who voluntarily come forward to render their services in the area 
of child care and development to help the local community for which they are paid honorarium. 
This honorarium is increased from time to time. From 1 st October, 2018, Government of India has 
enhanced the honorarium of AWWs at Anganwadi centres (AWCs) from Rs.3,000/ - to Rs.4,500/- 
per month and AWHs from Rs.1,500/- to Rs.2,250/- per month as per the defined cost sharing ratio 
between the Centre and States  and UTs. In addition, States and UTs are also paying additional 
monetary incentives and top ups to these functionaries from their own resources which vary from 
State to State. Details of additional top ups provided by States and UTs are at Annexure.  

Besides, performance linked incentive of Rs.500/ - per month is provided to AWWs and Rs.250/ - 
per month to AWHs. 
Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, AWWs have been technologically 
empowered with the provision of smartphones for efficient monitoring and delivery of services. 
Poshan Tracker which is a mobile phone application that has digitized physical reg isters used by 
Anganwadi workers. This improves the quality of their work while simultaneously enabling them 
for real-time monitoring of all activities going on in the Anganwadis.   
To incentivize and encourage the AWWs and AWHs, various initiatives have been undertaken 
including the following: 
i. Promotion: Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, promotional 
opportunities for AWWs and AWHs have been enhanced. 50% posts of AWWs are to be 
filled by AWHs with 5 years of experience and 50% posts of Supervisors are to be filled 
by promotion of AWWs with 5 years of experience subject to fulfilment of other criteria.  
ii. Leave: 20 days’ annual leave and paid maternity absence of 180 days and paid absence on 
abortion/ miscarriage once for 45 days.  
iii. State Governments and UT Administrations have been requested to encourage eligible 
AWWs and AWHs to get  themselves enrolled under the Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi 
Mandhan (PM -SYM) Pension Scheme, which is a voluntary and contributory pension 
scheme for the unorganized sector in the country to ensure old age protection.  
iv. Social Security Insurance Schemes: Insurance benefits have been provided to AWWs and 
AWHs under Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) for life cover worth 
Rs.2.00 lakh (covers life risk, death due to any reason) in the age group of 18 to 50 year s 
and under Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana for accidental cover of Rs.2.00 Lakh 
(accidental death and permanent full disability) /Rs.1.00 Lakh (partial but permanent 
disability) in the age group of 18 -59 years. 
v. Retirement date: States and UTs have been requested to adopt a uniform retirement date 
i.e 30 th April of each year with respect to AWWs and AWHs to ensure proper human 
resource planning. 
vi. Annual Healthcare coverage of Rs. 5 Lakhs under Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan 
Arogya Yojana (AB -PMJAY) to all AWWs and AWHs in pursuance to budget 
announcement in FY 2024 -25.  
Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 is a Centrally Sponsored scheme. The Central 
Government is responsible for policy and planning and the State Governments/UT Administrations 
are responsible for day-to-day program implementation of the scheme.

UNSTARRED QUESTION NO-2276
ANSWERED ON-31/07/2026
ACTION AGAINST CROSS-BORDER TERRORISM
2276. SMT. PRATIMA MONDAL
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state:-
(a) the details of measurable diplomatic outcomes which Government has 
secured in terms of  stronger international action against cross-border  
terrorism and greater accountability for States that continue to shelter or 
support terrorist infrastructure;
(b) the details of framework that guides the Government in reconciling  
competing  geopolitical  interests  without  diluting  India's  strategic 
autonomy as it balances strategic partnerships with the United States,  
Russia and Europe while simultaneously engaging through BRICS and the 
SCO; and
(c) the diplomatic initiatives undertaken by the Government to address  
the growing strategic convergence between China and Pakistan following 
reports of Chinese support to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor and the  

                                                                            2
manner  in  which  it  intend  to  safeguard  India's  long-term  security 
interests?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
(SHRI KIRTI VARDHAN SINGH)
(a)  The Government has been sensitising other countries, on an ongoing 
basis, on the issue of  cross-border terrorism emanating from Pakistan  
during various high level and other official visits. The Government has also 
set up Joint Working Groups (JWGs) on Counter Terrorism with 31 coun-
tries and 6 multilateral groupings where such issues are regularly taken  
up. Due to these persistent efforts, the global community has a greater  
understanding and appreciation of India’s concerns on cross-border ter -
rorism. Several countries have called upon Pakistan to not allow its ter -
ritory to be used for terrorism in any manner. 
India’s actions to defend itself against terrorism following the Pahalgam  
terror attack on 22 April 2025 has been recognised by many nations. The  
condemnation  of  the  Pahalgam  terror  attack  was  also  reflected  in 
outcome documents at various multilateral fora, including the UNSC Press 
Statement of  25 April 2025, 4th India-Central Asia Foreign Ministers’  

                                                                            3
Dialogue on 06 June 2025, the FATF Public Document on 16 June 2025,  
the Joint Statement of QUAD Foreign Ministers Meeting on 01 July 2025  
and  the  BRICS  Leaders’  Summit  Declaration  on  06  July  2025.   The 
Resistance  Front  (TRF),  a  proxy  of  the  Pakistan-based  terrorist 
organization Lashkar-e-Tayyiba (LeT), which  was involved in Pahalgam  
terror attack, was designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO)  
and  Specially  Designated  Global  Terrorist  (SDGT)  by  the  US  
Administration on 18 July 2025. Similarly, the 36 th UNSC 1267 Sanctions  
Committee Monitoring report dated 24 July 2025 made reference to TRF’s 
links to the Pahalgam terrorist attack.
  
India’s efforts over the years have led to the listing of  many terrorist  
entities and individuals who find shelter in Pakistan and are also engaged 
in terrorism against India by the United Nations (UN), the European Union 
and other countries. Tawahur Husssain Rana was extradited by the United 
States on 09 April 2025 to face trial in India for his role in planning the  
2008 Mumbai terrorist attacks.  
India  has  also  consistently  highlighted  Pakistan’s  deficiencies  in 
preventing  financial  support  to  terrorists,  contributing  to  sustained 
international scrutiny of terrorist networks operating from its territory.  

                                                                            4
Pakistan was placed in FATF Grey list three times with the last one being 
from June 2018-October 2022. As a result of FATF scrutiny, Pakistan has  
been forced to take some action against well-known terrorists, including  
those involved in attacks against the international community in Mumbai  
on 26/11. 
(b)  India’s foreign policy is guided by its overarching national interest.  
Strategic autonomy is an important strand of our foreign policy. India’s  
relationship with any country stands on its own footing and is independent 
of  the  relations  of  these  countries  with  third  countries.  India’s 
engagement in BRICS and the SCO is consistent with its foreign policy  
objectives without affecting its bilateral partnership with other countries.
(c) The Government of India closely monitors all developments having a  
bearing on India’s national security and takes all necessary measures to  
safeguard it. The Government remains committed to protecting India’s  
national interests and ensuring comprehensive national security across  
all domains.
*****

(c) whether cases of diversion, black marketing or hoarding of fertilisers have been 
detected in the said State during the last three years, if so, the details thereof along 
with the action taken thereon, year-wise;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS & FERTILIZERS

(a) to (e) Following steps are taken by the Government every season for ensuring 
timely and adequate supply of fertilizers across the States/UTs: 
I. Before the commencement of each cropping season, Department of Agriculture 
and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with all the State Governments, assesses 

the State-wise & month-wise requirement of fertilizers. On the basis of requirement 
projected by DA&FW, Department of Fertilizers (DoF) allocates adequate quantities of 
fertilizers to States by issuing monthly supply plan and continuously monitors the 
availability. 
 
II. The movement of all major subsidized fertilizers is monitored throughout the 
country by an on-line web-based monitoring system called integrated Fertilizer 
Management System (iFMS). 
 
III. The gap between demand (requirement) and production for Urea & other fertilizer 
is met through imports. The import for the season is also finalized well in advance to 
ensure timely availability.  
 
IV. The State Governments are regularly advised to coordinate with manufacturers 
and importers for streamlining the supplies through timely placement of indents. 
 
V. Regularly coordinate with the Ministry of Railways for giving sufficient rakes, 
priority to fertilizers and for timely evacuation of rakes for States. 
 
VI. The distribution of fertilizers within the State at district level is done by the State 
Government.

entries.t: Diagnostic facilities in PHCs and SHCs
entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE
LOK SABHA
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 2280
TO BE ANSWERED ON 31st JULY,2026
DIAGNOSTIC FACILITIES IN PHCs AND SHCs
2280. SHRI JAGADISH SHETTAR:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has taken any measures to overcome the issues concerning Primary
Health Centres (PHCs), Sub-Health Centres (SHCs), critical and infrastructure deficits, severe
shortage of medical specialist and lack of diagnostic facilities in the country; and
(b) if so, the details thereof?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) & (b): Public Health is a State subject. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare provides
technical and financial support to the States/UTs to strengthen the public healthcare services and
to promote disease prevention, based on the proposals received in the form of Programme
Implementation Plans (PIPs) under National Health Mission (NHM). Government of India
provides approval for the proposals in the form of Record of Proceedings (RoPs) as per norms &
available resources.
Health Dynamics of India (HDI), is an annual publication, based on healthcare administrative
data reported by States/UTs. Details of availability of doctors, nurses, other healthcare personnel
and health infrastructure across the country, State/UT-wise, may be accessed through the HMIS
portal under Publications at the following link of HDI 2023-24:
https://hmis.mohfw.gov.in
Through 1.86 lakh AAMs, comprehensive primary healthcare is provided by strengthening Sub
Health Centres (SHCs) and Primary Health Centres (PHCs). These AAMs provide preventive,
promotive, rehabilitative and curative care for an expanded range of services encompassing

reproductive and child healthcare services, Communicable diseases, Non-communicable diseases
and other health issues.
PM-Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM), launched with an outlay of
Rs. 64,180 crore, focuses on developing capacities of health systems and institutions across the
country. PM-ABHIM aims to support for infrastructure development for SHCs, Urban AAMs,
Support for Block Public Health Units (BPHUs), Integrated District Public Health Laboratories
(IPHL) and Critical Care Hospital Blocks (CCB). The Fifteenth Finance Commission (FC-XV)
had recommended grants through Local Governments for specific components of the health
sectors.
The Government of India has taken number of initiatives in the form of incentives and
honorarium to the medical professionals for encouraging better service delivery in rural and
remote areas across the country, which include:
i. Hard Area Allowance to specialist doctors for serving in rural and remote areas so that they
find it attractive to serve in public health facilities in such areas.
ii. States are also allowed to offer negotiable salary to attract specialist including flexibility in
strategies such as “You Quote We Pay”.
iii. Non-monetary incentives such as preferential admission in postgraduate courses for staff
serving in difficult areas and improving accommodation arrangement in rural areas have also
been introduced under NHM.
iv. Multi-skilling of doctors is supported under NHM to overcome the shortage of specialists
such as Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (CEmONC) and Life Saving
Anaesthesia Skills (LSAS).
Under Free Diagnostics Service Initiative, Government of India provides financial support to
States/UTs for essential pathological and radiological diagnostic services at all public health
facilities upto District level. This includes support for 14 tests at Sub Health Centre- Ayushman
Arogya Mandirs (SHC-AAMs), 63 tests at Primary Health Centre- Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
(PHC-AAMs), 97 tests at Community Health Centres (CHCs), 111 tests at Sub District Hospitals
(SDHs) and 134 tests at District Hospitals (DHs).
To improve health services in public health facilities, the Government of India has laid down
Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) 2022. These standards include norms for services,
infrastructure, human resources, diagnostics, equipment, medicines etc. NHM provides support
to address these gaps, ensuring the reach and meeting of essential standards for these facilities.
National Quality Assurance Standards (NQAS) have also been launched for all health facilities
including AAMs for an improved service delivery.

entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA

INCIDENCE OF FOOD ADULTERATION IN MAHARASHTRA
2281. SHRI BHASKAR MURLIDHAR BHAGARE:
Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFAREbe pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has taken cognizance of the increasing incidence of food
adulteration across the country, if so, the details thereof along with the number of food
samples collected, samples found non-conforming and enforcement actions taken by the
Government in Maharashtra during the last three years and the current year, year-wise;
(b) the details of prosecutions launched, licences suspended or cancelled and penalties
imposed in Maharashtra against manufacturers, traders and vendors found guilty of food
adulteration;
(c) whether the Government has provided any financial or technical assistance for
strengthening food testing laboratories, mobile food testing units and surveillance
mechanisms in Maharashtra, particularly in its tribal and remote districts, if so, the details
thereof, district-wise;
(d) whether the Government has undertaken any special awareness and enforcement drives
against food adulteration in Maharashtra during festive seasons and in rural markets, if so,
the details thereof; and
(e) the measures taken by the Government to strengthen digital traceability, rapid food
testing
and consumer awareness to curb food adulteration in the said State?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTHAND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (e): Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is mandated to lay down
science based standards for articles of food and to regulate their manufacture, storage,
distribution, sale and import to ensure availability of safe and wholesome food for human

consumption. The implementation and enforcement of the Food Safety and Standards (FSS)
Act, 2006 is a shared responsibility between the Central and State Governments.
Details of enforcement action taken against all non-conforming food products
(including adulteration) in Maharashtra during the last three years are annexed at Annexure-I.
Details of the number of licences suspended and cancelled in Maharashtra during the last
three years are annexed at Annexure II.
FSSAI has undertaken following measures to strengthen the laboratory testing,
surveillance and consumer awareness regarding food safety standards across the country are
as:
 For the safety of the food and food products through testing, FSSAI has notified 259
National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) for
analysis of food samples and 24 Referral Food Laboratories for the analysis of appeal
samples. Out of these, 39 FSSAI’s notified food testing laboratories are located in
Maharashtra, comprising 05 State Food Testing Laboratories, 02 other Government
Laboratories, and 32 Private Laboratories. These laboratories belong to the
States/UTs, various Government Institutions/Departments and private entities. FSSAI
provides technical and financial support to the State Food Safety Authorities, to
strengthen the food testing infrastructure in States & UTs.
 FSSAI has also provided assistance under the scheme “Strengthening of Food Testing
System in the Country including provision of Mobile Food Testing Labs'' (SoFTeL) to
various States and UTs. Assistance is provided to the Food and Drug Administration
(FDA) Laboratories at Mumbai & Chhatrapati. Sambhajinagar under SoFTeL
initiative, amounting to Rs. 19.21 Crore.
 To strengthen the laboratory capacity, from 2017 to till date FSSAI has conducted 222
training programmes for its notified food testing laboratories in which 3937
participants have been trained.
 Mobile Food Testing Laboratory (MFTL) or “Food Safety on Wheels” (FSW)
provides the widest outreach for food testing, training and awareness programme,
especially in the villages, towns and remote areas. Currently, 305 FSWs are deployed
across 35 States/UTs. The State of Maharashtra has 02 MFTLs.
 The "Magic Box" is a compact and user-friendly kit containing simple, rapid test
methods to detect common food adulterants in seven different food commodities. It

aims to identify adulteration in everyday food items such as milk, spices, oils, and
grains.
 Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test (DART) book covers 44 tests that can be
performed easily at household level with the help of water and simple solutions like
tincture of iodine for food products like Milk & Milk Products, Oils & Fats, Sugar &
Confectionary, Food Grains & its products, Spices & Condiments etc. These tests
also include sensory evaluation tests for establishing authentication of food products.
DART book depicts the differences between pure and adulterated food product
through pictorial representation.

Condition of AWCs in Rajasthan  
  
†2282. Shri Bhajan Lal Jatav:  
  
Will the Minister of Women and Child Development be pleased to state:  
  
(a) the total number of Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) buildings sanctioned and the number of 
Anganwadi Centres functioning in dilapidated, damaged, rented or building -less premises in

(b) whether any special Central assistance or special project has been proposed for the

(c) the level at which accountability would be fixed in the event of any accident or injury to 
children, pregnant women or lactating mothers at Anganwadi Centres  functioning in dilapidated

ANSWER 
  
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRIMATI SAVITRI THAKUR)  
  
(a) to (c) The district wise number of Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) functioning under Mission 
Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 including State of Rajasthan is available on the Poshan 
Tracker public dashboard at the link: https://www.poshantracker.in/statistics . 
Under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, there is a provision of construction of AWC 
building in convergence with the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee 
Scheme (MGNREGS). 
  
Further, States/UTs have also been advised to continue to tap funds for construction of AWC 
buildings from various schemes such as Member of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme 
(MPLADS), Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), Finance Commission  Grants to 

Panchayati Raj Institutions, Multi - Sectoral Development Programme (MSDP) of Ministry of 
Minority Affairs, etc. 
  
Under PM-JANMAN (Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan), a total of 2,500 
Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) have been sanctioned for construction in PVTG (Particularly 
Vulnerable Tribal Groups) areas out of which 51 AWCs has been sanctioned for construc tion to 
the state of Rajasthan. 
  
Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DAJGUA) launched by the Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs (MoTA ) focusses on convergence, outreach and saturation in tribal majority villages. 
Under DAGJUA, 875 AWCs have been sanctioned for construction out of which 135 AWCs has 
been sanctioned for construction to the state of Rajasthan including 9 AWCs to the Distri ct of 
Karauli and 1 AWC to the District of Dholpur.  
  
Directions have been issued to States/UTs to co -locate Anganwadi Centres, which are running on 
rent without sufficient infrastructure, at nearby Primary Schools, where space is available. 
Guidelines for Co -locating Anganwadi Centres within Government Primary Schools have been 
issued jointly with Ministry of Education.  
  
Also, in order to improve the infrastructure facilities at AWCs, funds @Rs.17,000/ - for providing 
drinking water facilities and @Rs.36,000/ - for construction of toilets are provided to States and 
UTs.  
  
Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0 is a Centrally Sponsored scheme. The 
implementation of the scheme falls under the ambit of State Governments and UTs' administration. 
The matter regarding infrastructure is regularly taken up with them through sustained engagements 
and video conferences so as to ensure uninterrupted delivery of services to the beneficiaries.

UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 2286
TO BE ANSWERED ON 31ST JULY,2026
INCREASING SUICIDE AMONG STUDENTS
2286. SMT. DHANORKAR PRATIBHA SURESH:
Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of Education are jointly
proposing to implement any national policy to reduce mental stress among students in schools,
colleges and professional coaching institutions in the country, if so, the details thereof; and
(b) the steps taken/proposed to be taken by the Government to make it mandatory to appoint
qualified psychiatrists and counsellors in every educational institution across the country and to
provide counselling services for parents?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND
FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) and (b) To address the burden of mental disorders, the Government of India is implementing
the National Mental Health Programme (NMHP) in the country. The District Mental Health
Programme (DMHP) component of the NMHP has been sanctioned for implementation in 767
districts for which support is provided to States/UTs through the National Health Mission.
Under DMHP, targeted interventions are conducted for school and college students. Under
Targeted interventions, the following activities are carried out in the districts across the country,
such as life skills education & counselling in schools, training of college teachers to work as
counsellors, counselling of out of school children having mental health problems/ adolescent
mental health program, etc.
The Government is also taking steps to strengthen mental healthcare services at primary
healthcare level. The Government has upgraded more than 1.8 lakh Sub Health Centres (SHCs)
and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) to Ayushman Arogya Mandirs. Mental health services have
been added in the packages of services under Comprehensive Primary Health Care provided at
these Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
“Emotional Wellbeing and Mental Health” is incorporated as a dedicated module under
Ayushman Bharat School Health & Wellness Programme. Health and Wellness Ambassadors

(Teachers) are trained on mental health along with other thematic areas of the programme, take
interactive sessions with the students and percolate the messages through weekly sessions
promoting joyful learning.
The Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK) of the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare
through its interventions viz. Adolescent Friendly Health Clinics (AFHC), Peer Education
Programme and Adolescent Health and Wellness Days (AH&WD) creates awareness on mental
health issues and provides counselling services. Peer Educators form groups of 15-20 boys and
girls in the community and conduct weekly one to two hour participatory sessions on adolescent
health including mental health and wellbeing.
Ministry of Education (MoE), has launched an initiative, Manodarpan, with the aim to provide
psychosocial support to students, their families and teachers across the country, for mental health
and well-being . All activities undertaken under the Manodarpan initiative are aimed towards
supporting the metal health and well-being of students from schools, colleges and universities,
including those students who are preparing for competitive examinations.
Besides the above, the Government has launched a “National Tele Mental Health Programme”
on 10th October, 2022, to further improve access to quality mental health counselling and care
services in the country. As on 27.07.2026, 36 States/ UTs have set up 53 Tele MANAS Cells and
have started tele mental health services. More than 42 lakh calls have been handled on the
helpline number.
As the information received from Ministry of Education, CBSE has strengthened counselling
framework in schools through a structured dual-counsellor mode vide notification dated
19.01.2026. Under this framework, schools are required to appoint the following counsellors as
to address both psychosocial and career-related needs of students:
i. Counselling & Wellness Teacher (Socio-Emotional Counsellor)
ii. Career Counsellor.
CBSE has also implemented the Counselling Hub & Spoke School Model to strengthen school-
based counselling support and introduced the Parenting Calendar to promote awareness and early
identitification of students’ socio-emotional needs through active parent-school engagement.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE

TO BE ANSWERED ON 31st JULY,2026
SHORTAGE OF MEDICAL STAFF IN HEALTH CENTRES IN MAHARASHTRA
2287. DR. AMOL RAMSING KOLHE:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the existing network of Sub-Health Centres (SHCs), Primary Health Centres
(PHCs) and Community Health Centres (CHCs) in Maharashtra meets the Indian Public
Health Standards (IPHS) and prescribed population norms, if so, the details thereof, district-
wise;
(b) the number of sanctioned, functional and vacant SHCs, PHCs, CHCs, Sub-District
Hospitals and District Hospitals in the State, including Pune District, along with the shortages
of doctors, specialists, nurses and paramedical staff in the said institutions;
(c) whether the Government has undertaken any assessment of the healthcare infrastructure
requirements of Pune District, in view of its rapidly growing urban and peri-urban population
and if so, the details thereof;
(d) the corrective measures taken by the Union Government to bridge infrastructure and
manpower gaps, particularly in the tribal, hilly, drought-prone and aspirational districts of
Maharashtra; and
(e) the timeline fixed by the Union Government for achieving full compliance with IPHS
norms across the State?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (e): Public Health’ & ‘Hospitals’ are State subjects. The primary responsibility of the
availability of healthcare facilities and human resources in various public health facilities in
the country lies with the respective State Governments.
The National Health Mission (NHM) provides support for improvement in health
infrastructure, availability of adequate human resources in health facilities, to improve
availability and accessibility to quality healthcare across the country including Maharashtra.
Under NHM, this Ministry provides technical and financial support to the States/UTs,
including tribal, hilly, drought-prone and aspirational districts of Maharashtra, to strengthen
the public healthcare system in rural areas, based on the proposals received in the form of

Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs). Government of India provides approval for the
proposals received in the form of Record of Proceedings (RoPs) as per norms & available
resources.
The Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) have been developed by MoHFW for primary and
secondary healthcare facilities which provides a set of uniform standards, including norms for
services, infrastructure, human resources, diagnostics, equipment, medicines etc, envisaged to
improve the quality of health care delivery in the country. They are used as the reference
point for public health care infrastructure planning and up-gradation in the States and UTs.
Health Dynamics of India (HDI) is an annual publication, based on healthcare administrative
data reported by States/UTs. Details of availability and shortfall of health infrastructure
including Sub-Health Centres (SHCs), Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and Community
Health Centres (CHCs) and doctors, specialists, nurses, paramedical staff across the country
including Pune district in Maharashtra, State/UT-wise, may be accessed through the HMIS
portal under Publications at the following link of HDI 2023-24:
https://hmis.mohfw.gov.in
To facilitate the assessment of public health facilities, MoHFW has developed an Open Data
Kit (ODK), an Android-based application. This application allows States and UTs to conduct
a baseline assessment of their healthcare facilities, identify gaps, and implement timely
corrective measures by achieving compliance to provide all essential services and work
towards desirable standards.
Under NHM, the performance of various health programmes including gaps in health
infrastructure in all the States/UTs including Pune district of Maharashtra in view of its
rapidly growing urban and peri-urban population, through review meetings, mid-term reviews
of key deliverables, field visits of senior officials, promoting performance by setting up
benchmarks for service delivery & rewarding achievements etc. Common Review Missions
(CRM) are conducted annually to assess and monitor the progress and implementation status
under the scheme.
Under NHM, norms have been relaxed for tribal/hilly/hard-to-reach areas to strengthen
healthcare access. Population criteria for setting up of SHCs, PHCs and CHCs have been
reduced to 3,000, 20,000 and 80,000 respectively. One Accredited Social Health Activist
(ASHA) is allowed per habitation instead of per 1,000 population.
A total of 1.86 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs) including 13,457 AAMs in
Maharashtra have been operationalized by strengthening SHCs and PHCs. These AAMs
provide preventive, promotive, rehabilitative and curative care for an expanded range of
services. The AAMs incrementally provide 12 package

States/UTs to strengthen their healthcare systems, based on the requirements posed by
States/UTs in their Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) within their overall Resource

Proceedings (RoPs) as per norms & available resources.
Health Dynamics of India (HDI), is an annual publication, based on healthcare administrative

across the country, State/UT-wise, may be accessed through the HMIS portal under
Publications at the following link of HDI 2023-24: https://hmis.mohfw.gov.in
(d) Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) are supported under National Health Mission (NHM) to
provide outreach services in remote tribal regions with difficult terrain which are underserved

and inaccessible. Under NHM, norms have been relaxed for tribal/hilly/hard-to-reach areas to
strengthen healthcare access. Up to 4 MMUs per district are permitted in tribal and hard-to-
reach areas, compared to 2 in plain districts. As per NHM-MIS report, a total of 1,546 MMUs

Under National Ambulance Service, 3,287 Advanced Life Support (ALS), 15,472 Basic Life
Support (BLS), 3,912 Patient Transport Vehicle (PTV), 19 Boat Ambulances, 81 Bike
Emergency Response Vehicles and 5,701 other empanelled vehicles are supported under

2289. SHRI RAJABHAU PARAG PRAKASH WAJE:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has assessed the reasons why Government hospitals continue to
face severe shortages of doctors, specialists, nurses, paramedical staff, essential medicines,
diagnostic facilities and critical medical equipment despite increased public expenditure and
multiple health sector initiatives, if so, the details thereof;
(b) the details of sanctioned and vacant posts of healthcare personnel, availability of essential
medicines, ICU beds, diagnostic facilities and critical equipment in Government hospitals in
the country during the last five years, State-wise;
(c) whether the Government has evaluated the impact of these shortages on patient care,
treatment delays, referral rates, maternal and infant mortality and out-of-pocket healthcare
expenditure if so, the details and the findings thereof; and
(d) the specific policy measures, budgetary allocations, accountability mechanisms and
timebound roadmap proposed to fill up vacancies, modernise public hospitals and ensure
equitable access to affordable, quality healthcare across the country?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND
FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (d): Health is a State subject. The primary responsibility of strengthening public
healthcare system, including vacant posts lies with the respective State/UT Governments. The
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare provides technical and financial support to the
States/UTs to strengthen the public healthcare system in rural areas based on the proposals
received in the form of Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) under National Health
Mission. Government of India provides approval for the proposal in the form of Record of
Proceedings (RoPs) as per norms & available resources. States/ UTs to ensure availability of
HR by creating adequate number of regular posts as per the Indian Public Health Standards
(IPHS) in the long run and using NHM posts in the short to medium term to fill critical gaps.

The NHM supplements the regular human resources by filling up the gaps in human
resources in secondary and primary care facilities (District Hospital and below) as per IPHS.
The details of doctors, specialists, physicians, nurses and paramedical staff in
Government hospitals and health centres across the country and their vacancies State/UT-
wise can be accessed at the following link of HDI 2023-24:
https://www.mohfw-dohfw.gov.in/static/uploads/2026/05/57202cf30629539e4d0fb0a2f700ac
62.pdf
This Ministry supports ‘Free Diagnostics Service Initiative’ programme under NHM
with the aim to provide accessible and affordable pathological and radiological diagnostics
services closer to the community, which in turn reduces the Out-of-Pocket Expenditure
(OOPE). Diagnostics services are provided free of cost at all levels of public health facilities
(14 tests at Sub Centers, 63 at Primary Health Centers, 97 at Community Health Centres, 111
test at Sub District Hospitals and 134 tests at District Hospitals).
Under NHM, following types of incentives and honorarium are provided for
encouraging doctors, specialists, nurses and paramedical staff to practice in rural and remote
areas of the country to address the shortage of staff:
• Hard area, including rural and tribal areas, are given allowances to specialist doctors
for serving in rural and remote areas and for their residential quarters so that they find it
attractive to serve in public health facilities in such areas.
• Honorarium to Gynecologists/ Emergency Obstetric Care (EmOC) trained,
Pediatricians & Anesthetist/ Life Saving Anaesthesia Skills (LSAS) trained doctors is also
provided to increase availability of specialists for conducting Cesarean Sections in rural &
remote area.
• Incentives like special incentives for doctors, incentive for Auxiliary Nurse and
Midwife (ANM) for ensuring timely Antenatal Checkup (ANC) checkup and recording,
incentives for conducting Adolescent Reproductive and Sexual Health activities.
• States are also allowed to offer negotiable salary to attract specialist including
flexibility in strategies such as “You Quote We Pay”.

• Non-Monetary incentives such as preferential admission in post graduate courses for
staff serving in difficult areas and improving accommodation arrangement in rural areas have
also been introduced under NHM.
• Multi-skilling of doctors is supported under NHM to overcome the shortage of
specialists. Skill upgradation of existing HR is another major strategy under NRHM for
achieving improvement in health outcomes.

through a robust, multi-layered framework that includes review of State-wise Key

PRESCRIPTION FOR MEDICINAL SYRUPS
2292. SHRI SUDAMA PRASAD:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has assessed the impact of the prescription only requirement for
medicinal syrups on patient residing of rural, tribal and remote areas where access to
registered medical practitioners is limited, if so, the details thereof; and
(b) whether any monitoring mechanism has been established by the Government to prevent
the illegal sale of syrup-based medicines without a prescription in the country and if so, the
details thereof?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SMT. ANUPRIYAPATEL)
(a) & (b): As per the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and Drugs Rules, 1945, all drugs
including cough syrups covered under Schedule X, H and/or H1 are required to be sold by
retail on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) only. Further, Schedule
K to the said Rules provided an exemption for sale of cough syrups in villages with a
population not exceeding 1,000 persons and where no dealer was licensed under the said Act.
However, the Government vide notification G.S.R 477 (E) dated 09.06.2026, has amended
the Drugs Rules, 1945, withdrawing the said exemption to enhance regulatory control and
promote safe use of cough syrup in the interest of patient safety.
However, drugs supplied by Multipurpose workers attached to Primary Health
Centres/Sub-Centres, Community Health V olunteersunder the Rural Health Scheme, Nurses
Auxiliary Nurses, Midwives and Lady Health Visitors attached to Urban Family Welfare
Centres/Primary Health Centres/Sub-Centres, Anganwadi Workers and Community Health
Officers at Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres are permitted under Schedule K to
dispense prescribed drugs without a sale license.

State Licensing Authorities carryout periodic inspections or as per risk-based
approach from time to time of the licensed premises for verification of compliance with the
provisions of the Act and rules thereunder. Actions such as suspension and cancellation of
licences, prosecutions in the court of law are taken against the erring firms by the State
Licensing Authorities.

2293. SHRI SUKANTAKUMAR PANIGRAHI:
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether it is a fact that the Government's visionary expansion of Ayushman Arogya
Mandirs has successfully enhanced primary healthcare access across the nation, with centers
operational as of 2026, if so, the details thereof;
(b) whether the Government has analyzed that the systematic release and utilization of funds
during the last three years have significantly improved healthcare delivery standards across
the country, if so, the details thereof;
(c) whether the Government proposes to further strengthen these Mandirs in aspirational
districts like Kandhamal, Odisha, by integrating advanced digital diagnostics and AI-driven
healthcare services to bridge the urban-rural divide, if so, the details thereof; and
(d) whether the Government, building upon its commendable national progress, is likely to
consider a time-bound roadmap to enhance infrastructure and workforce capability in these
tribal-dominated areas to ensure universal health coverage and improved medical outcomes
for the local population, if so, the details thereof?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) to (d): The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare provides technical and financial
support to the States/UTs to strengthen the public healthcare system including primary and
district-level healthcare services, based on the proposals received in the form of Programme
Implementation Plans (PIPs) under National Health Mission (NHM). Government of India
provides approval for the proposal in the form of Record of Proceedings (RoPs) as per norms
& available resources. More than 1.86 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs) have been
operationalized by strengthening Sub Health Centres (SHCs) and Primary Health Centres
(PHCs) in the country. A total of 7,379 AAMs in Odisha including 221 AAMs in Kandhamal
district have been operationalized.
These AAMs provide preventive, promotive, rehabilitative and curative care for an expanded
range of services. The AAMs incrementally provide 12 package of primary health care
services across the country, encompassing Reproductive and child care services,
Communicable diseases, Non Communicable diseases (NCD), Palliative Care and elderly Care,

Care for common mental disorders, neurological conditions (epilepsy, dementia) and substance
use disorders management (tobacco, alcohol, drugs), Oral health, ENT care, and Basic
emergency care.
The Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) have been developed by MoHFW for primary and
secondary healthcare facilities which provides a set of uniform standards, including norms for
services, infrastructure, human resources, diagnostics, equipment, medicines etc, envisaged to
improve the quality of health care delivery in the country. They are used as the reference
point for public health care infrastructure planning and up-gradation in the States and UTs.
Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) aims to create an online platform enabling
interoperability of health data within the health ecosystem to create longitudinal electronic
health record of every citizen, to improve access to quality healthcare in aspirational districts
including Kandhamal.
The teleconsultation services, available at all operational AAMs across the country, enables
people to access the specialist services closer to their homes addressing concerns of physical
accessibility, shortage of service providers and to facilitate continuum of care.
In an effort to establish seamless data flow and continuity of care, MoHFW has launched
Swasth Bharat Portal - a centralized digital platform that provides single-window access to
multiple national health programs, thereby reducing the burden of data reporting on
healthcare providers and prioritizing patient care. It enables care providers to manage
beneficiary details through ABHA ID and view longitudinal health records across various
health programs.
The Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) aims to
support for infrastructure development for SHCs, Urban AAMs, Support for Block Public
Health Units (BPHUs), Integrated District Public Health Laboratories (IPHL) and Critical
Care Hospital Blocks (CCB) in the country including tribal-dominated areas. The Fifteenth
Finance Commission (FC-XV) had recommended grants through Local Governments for
specific components of the health sectors.
Under NHM, norms have been relaxed for tribal/hilly/hard-to-reach areas to strengthen
healthcare access. Population criteria for setting up of SHCs, PHCs and Community Health
Centres (CHCs) have been relaxed from 5,000, 30,000 and 1,20,000 to 3,000, 20,000 and
80,000 respectively. One Accredited Social Health Activ

Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government has reviewed the implementation of the Ayushman Bharat
Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) during the last three years, if so, the details
of the eligible beneficiaries, patients, who have availed treatment and empanelled hospitals
across the country, State-wise, particularly in Himachal Pradesh and the Shimla
Parliamentary constituency;
(b) the steps taken by the Government to expand health insurance coverage and to strengthen
primary healthcare services through the Ayushman Arogya Mandirs along with their current
status in Himachal Pradesh and the Shimla Parliamentary constituency;
(c) the current status of the integration of ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account), digital
health records and other digital health services under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission;
and
(d) whether the said scheme has reduced the Out-of-Pocket Expenditure on healthcare for the
people and the progress made towards the goal of Universal Health Coverage across the
country, particularly in Himachal Pradesh and the Shimla Parliamentary constituency, if so,

ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND
FAMILYWELFARE
(SHRI PRATAPRAOJADHA V)
(a) and (b): National Health Authority regularly reviews the implementation of Ayushman
Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) through periodic review meetings
with States/UTs to assess the progress of scheme implementation, beneficiary coverage,
hospital empanelment and scheme utilisation.
AB-PMJAY was launched in September 2018 and initially the scheme covered 10.74 crore
families identified under the Socio-Economic Caste Census, 2011, constituting the bottom
40% of India's population. In January 2023, the beneficiary base was revised from 10.74
crore to 12 crore families to account for India's decadal population growth. In March 2024,
approximately 37 lakh additional families of Accredited Social Health Activists, Anganwadi

Workers and Anganwadi Helpers were included under the scheme. The scheme was further
expanded in October 2024 to cover 6 crore senior citizens of age 70 years and above
belonging to 4.5 crore families irrespective of their socio-economic status.
As on 30.06.2026, a total of 37,413 hospitals are empanelled under the scheme, of which
14,761 hospitals have been empanelled during the last three years (FY 2023-24 to FY 2025-
26). The State/UT-wise and district-wise details of empanelled hospitals including Himachal
Pradesh can be accessed at https://hem.nha.gov.in/search
Further, as on 30.06.2026, a total of 12.69 crore hospital admission have been authorized
under the scheme, of which 7.14 crore hospital admission have been authorized during the
last three years (FY 2023-24 to FY 2025-26). The State/UT-wise details of hospital
admissions authorized including Himachal Pradesh during the same period are at Annexure.

ARBITRARY FEES AT PRIV ATECLINICS
†2295. SHRI RAJESH RANJAN:
Will the Minister of HEALTHAND FAMILYWELFARE be pleased to state:
(a) whether the Government is aware that private clinics, nursing homes and so-called super
multi-speciality hospitals in many States of the country are charging arbitrary fees from
patients, compelling them to undergo unnecessary ultrasound, MRI and other diagnostic tests
only at their affiliated centres and withholding the bodies of deceased patients for non-
payment of dues;
(b) if so, the details thereof;
(c) whether complaints regarding illegal collection of charges in the name of ventilator
support and repeated consultation fees being charged by the same doctor have come to the
notice of the Government, if so, the details thereof;
(d) whether the Union Government has any plan to establish national standards/guidelines for
treatment rates, testing standards and consultation period in these hospitals and to compel the
State Governments to follow the same; and
(e) if so, the details thereof?
ANSWER
THE MINISTER OF STATEIN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY
WELFARE
(SMT. ANUPRIYAPATEL)
(a) to (e): ‘Health’ being a State subject, the primary responsibility to address the issue of
charging of arbitrary fees from patients, compelling them to undergo unnecessary ultrasound,
MRI and other diagnostic tests only at their affiliated centres and withholding the bodies of
deceased patients lies with the respective States/UTs.
Nonetheless, the Government of India enacted the Clinical Establishments (Registration
and Regulation) Act, 2010 (CE Act) and notified the Clinical Establishments (Central
Government) Rules, 2012 amended in 2018 and 2020 (CE Rules) to provide for registration
and regulation of Government (except those of Armed Forces) as well as private clinical

establishments belonging to recognized systems of medicine. As per CE Act, the clinical
establishments are required to fulfill the conditions of minimum standards for each type of
service provided. The CE Act is adopted by 19 States/UTs (12 States, viz., Arunachal Pradesh,
Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Rajasthan, Sikkim,
Telangana, Uttarakhand & Uttar Pradesh and 7 UTs, viz., Andaman & Nicobar Islands,
Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh,
Lakshadweep & Puducherry). For registration of clinical establishments, the CE Rules, inter-
alia, stipulates the following:
(i) every clinical establishment shall display the rates charged for each type of service
provided and facilities available, for the benefit of the patients at a conspicuous
place in the local as well as in English language.
(ii) the clinical establishments shall charge the rates for each type of procedures and
services within the range of rates determined and issues by the Central
Government in consultation with the State Governments. In this connection, the
Central Government has held multiple consultations with the States/UTs. The
matter is, at present, sub-judice in the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India.
(iii) The clinical establishments shall ensure compliance of the Standard Treatment
Guidelines.
‘Health’ being a State subject, the States / UTs which have adopted the CE Act are
primarily responsible for enforcing/implementing the provisions of the CE Act in the
respective States/UTs. The Act has empowered a registering authority at the district level
under the chairmanship of the District Collector / District Magistrate to take actions including
imposing penalties in respect of violation of its provisions. The Act also provides for
cancellation of registration, if the provisions of the Act are not complied with. Data and
details with regard to action taken against such clinical establishments are not maintained
centrally. The clinical establishments in the States/UTs, which have not adopted and
implemented the CE Act, are registered and regulated by the respective State Acts.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS & FERTILIZERS

(a):     At present, there is no such proposal of Ramagundam Fertilizers and 
Chemicals Limited (RFCL) under consideration in the Department of Fertilizers. 
 
(b) & (c):    The following steps are taken by the Government in every season for 
ensuring timely and adequate supply of fertilizers across the States/UTs, including 
the State of Telangana: 
 
I. Before the commencement of each cropping season, Department of Agriculture 
and Farmers Welfare (DA&FW), in consultation with all the State Governments, 
assesses the State-wise & month-wise requirement of fertilizers. On the basis of 
requirement projected by DA&FW, Department of Fertilizers (DoF) allocates 
adequate quantities of fertilizers to States by issuing monthly supply plan and 
continuously monitors the availability. 
 
 

 
 
-2- 
 
II. The movement of all major subsidized fertilizers is monitored throughout the 
country by an on-line web-based monitoring system called integrated Fertilizer 
Management System (iFMS). 
 
III. The State Governments are regularly advised to coordinate with 
manufacturers and importers for streamlining the supplies through timely 
placement of indents. 
 
IV. Regular coordination with the Ministry of Railways is undertaken for giving 
sufficient rakes, priority to fertilizers and for timely evacuation of rakes for States. 
 
V. The distribution of fertilizers within the State at district level is done by the 
concerned State government. 
 
                Further, to ensure an efficient and uninterrupted supply, Urea produced by 
RFCL, like that from all other indigenous manufacturing plants, is pooled at the 
national level and allocated to States based on their assessed requirements to 
ensure equitable distribution across the country.  
 
                Accordingly, the availability of fertilizers has remained adequate in the

science based standards for articles of food and to regulate their manufacture, storage,
distribution, sale and import to ensure availability of safe and wholesome food for human
consumption. The implementation and enforcement of the Food Safety and Standards (FSS)
Act, 2006 is a shared responsibility between the Central and State Governments.
FSSAI vide advisory dated 28.03.2024 has clarified that ‘Health Drink’ is not defined/
standardized anywhere under the FSS Act, 2006 or rules and regulations made thereunder.
Therefore, the food products licensed under 'Proprietary Food' with the nearest category-Dairy
Based Beverage Mix or Cereal Based Beverage Mix or Malt Based Beverage being sold in the
e-commerce website under the category ‘Health Drink’, ‘Energy Drink’ have been advised to
remove / de-link such drinks / beverages from the category of ‘Health Drinks / Energy Drinks’
on their website and place such products in the appropriate category as provided under the
extant law.

As per the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives)
Regulations, 2011 the Caffeinated Beverage “shall contain not less than 145 mg per liter and
not more than 300 mg per litre total caffeine from whatever sources it may be derived in the
formulation of the product”. Further, the label of the product is required to carry the
declaration, consume not more than 500 ml per day." The standards are specified based on
scientific risk assessment carried out by the independent Scientific Panels and the Scientific
Committee of FSSAI, taking into account available scientific evidence, dietary exposure and
country-specific requirements and are substantially harmonized with the internationally
accepted norms.
FSSAI has taken many measures to curb adulteration in the food products such as
awareness campaigns like “#No To Adulteration”, “How to Check for Adulteration” and also
provided funds for Mobile Food Testing Laboratory (MFTL) or “Food Safety on wheels”
(FSW), Food Safety Magic Boxes. The FSSAI has approved Rapid Analytical Food Testing
(RAPID) Kits and published Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test (DART) Booklet to detect
adulteration.
Further, 15 notices have been issued to FBOs during FY 2026–27 for violations of the
Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020. Details of enforcement
action taken by the State/UT Food Safety Authorities against non-conforming food products
including cases of adulteration, during 2025-26, are as under:-

(a) to (e) Under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), a Satellite Centre of
All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Bhubaneswar has been set up at Balasore with

Kisan Credit Card Loans 
†2301. SHRI NEERAJ MAURYA:  
SHRI HARENDRA SINGH MALIK:  
MS IQRA CHOUDHARY:  
SHRI LALJI VERMA: 
 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government is aware that small farmers in the rural areas of Uttar Pradesh are 
being deprived of Kisan Credit Card loans carrying an effective interest rate of 4 per cent due 
to the stringent conditions relating to Credit Information Bureau India Limited (CIBIL) score 
and no-dues certificates imposed by banks thereby forcing them into the debt trap of private 
moneylenders, if so, the details thereof; 
(b) whether there is an inordinate delay by the banks in the renewal of existing loans thereby 
increasing the cost of farming despite the announcement in the Budget 2026-27 to increase the 
Kisan Credit Card loan limit from Rs. 3 lakh to Rs. 5 lakh, if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether farmers who repay their loans on time are facing technical hurdles in availing the 
benefit of the 3 per cent prompt repayment incentive due to slow data feeding on the Kisan 
Loan Portal, if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) whether the Government proposes to take punitive action against the banks which forcibly 
impose an insurance policy or any other financial product while sanctioning crop loans and if 
so, the details thereof ? 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI PANKAJ CHAUDHARY)  
(a) In a deregulated credit environment, lenders take credit decisions as per their Board 
approved policies and the applicable regulatory guidelines. Moreover, banks and financial 
institutions obtain credit information reports of borrowers from one or more credit information 
companies (CICs) so that credit decisions may be taken on the basis of information available 
in the system. Such reports are primarily used for due diligence, particularly to assess the 
repayment history and any existing defaults of bor rowers with other lending institutions.  

However, RBI has not indicated any minimum credit score requirement from borrowers for 
sanctioning of loans including through Kisan Credit Cards.   
 
Further, in terms of RBI’s circular dated 28 January 2015, Schedul ed Commercial Banks 
(including Regional Rural Banks) have been advised to dispense with obtaining ‘No Due 
Certificate’ from the individual borrowers (including SHGs & JLGs) in rural and semi -urban 
areas for  all types of loans including loans under Government Sponsored Schemes, irrespective 
of the amount involved unless  the Government Sponsored Scheme itself provides for obtaining 
of ‘No Due Certificate’.   
 
(b) The review of loan limit provided through Kisan Credit Card is contingent upon the 
repayment made by the borrower and credit policy of the bank framed under the applicable 
regulatory guidelines. Moreover, SLBC Uttar Pradesh has informed that in order to provide 
uninterrupted crop finance to farmers, banks have been regularly advised to ensure timely  
renewal and review of KCC accounts in accordance with the extant guidelines.   
 
(c) Government has launched Kisan Rin Portal (KRP) in September 2023, enabling Aadhaar -
based beneficiary authentication and faster digital claim settlements under the Modified  
Interest Subvention Scheme (MISS) for loans availed through KCC. The said portal has 
significantly enhanced transparency, accountability and operational efficiency in the 
administration of Interest Subvention (IS) and Prompt Repayment Incentive (PRI) claims.  
 
(d) In terms of  Master Direction on Responsible Business Conduct Second Amendment 
Directions, 2026 issued by Reserve Bank of India, which is applicable from 01 January 2027, 
banks have been prohibited from compulsory bundling of another product/service with sale of 
the requested product/service by the customer. It stipulates the need for explicit customer 
consent while issuing insurance policy.  Further, as per the said direction, in cases where mis-
selling of a financial product / service is established based on customer complaint, banks shall 
refund the entire amount paid by the customer for purchase of the financial product / service 
and also intimate the customer about cancellation of the sale, wherever applicable. Bank shall 
also compensate the c ustomer, for any loss arising due to mis -selling, as per its approved 
policy.

2303. SHRI BABU SINGH KUSHWAHA: 
 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE be pleased to 
state:  
 
(a) whether Surha Tal Bird Sanctuary, located in Ballia, Uttar Pradesh has been 
notified/designated as a wetland and if so, the details thereof; 
 
(b) the details of funds allocated by the Government for the conservation, development and 
management of the said sanctuary and the amount actually utilized therefrom during the last 
three years, item-wise; 
 
(c) the expenditure incurred on conservation, habitat improvement, biodiversity enhancement, 
wetland management, water management, protection of migratory birds and other related 
activities during the said period; 
 
(d) whether the Government has launched any special scheme, project or Central assistance 
programme for the conservation of Surna Tal Bird Sanctuary biodiversity enhancement, 
wetland conservation and management and promotion of eco-tourism; and 
 
(e) if so, the details and present status thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND 
CLIMATE CHANGE 
 (SHRI KIRTI VARDHAN SINGH) 
 
(a) to (e) The Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary (Surha Tal Bird Sanctuary) has been 
designated as a Wetland of International Importance under Ramsar convention (Ramsar Site) 
in view of its ecological importance.  It is the 100th Ramsar site in the Country. The Ministry 
of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC), is currently implementing a 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) namely, the National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic 
Ecosystems (NPCA) for conservation and management of wetlands in the country on cost 
sharing basis between Central Government and respective State Governments. The scheme 
provides funds for the Integrated Management Plans (IMPs)/Framework Management Plans 
(FMPs) received from the States/UTs, including Uttar Pradesh, for conservation and 
management of wetlands. It aims at holistic conservation and restoration of wetlands for 
achieving the desired water quality enhancement, besides improvement in biodiversity and 

2 
 
ecosystems through an integrated and multi-disciplinary approach. The State Wetland 
Authority of Uttar Pradesh functions as an apex body for integrated management of wetlands 
and submits proposals under the NPCA scheme for consideration of the Ministry. Further 
Ministry provides financial assistance to the States/UTs under CSS "Development of Wildlife 
Habitats" for conservation and management of protected areas, conservation of wildlife outside 
protected areas and recovery of critically endangered species and its habitats as per the Annual 
Plan of Operation received from the States/UTs, including state of Uttar Pradesh. The financial 
assistance to the State/UTs includes activities for the protection and management of wildlife 
like patrolling, habitat management, awareness programme, maintenance of fire lines, 
engagement of protection watchers, Eco development and support for activities related to   eco-
tourism. The details of funds released/utilized during last three financial years to Jai 
Prakash  Narayan (Surah Tal) Bird Sanctuary in Uttar Pradesh under the CSS-Development of 
Wildlife Habitats are as given in Annexure. 
 
MoEF&CC has taken several steps for protection and preservation of wetlands across 
the country, which include, implementation of Ramsar Convention on wetlands, Wetlands 
(Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 under the provisions of the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986, a dedicated Wetlands Web Portal(https://indianwetlands.in), Mission 
Sahbhagita and Save Wetlands Campaign for peoples and stakeholders’ participation in the 
wetlands conservation and management, Amrit Dharohar initiative to promote unique 
conservation values of Ramsar sites. The four key components of Amrit Dharohar are Species 
and Habitat Conservation, Nature Tourism, Wetlands Livelihoods and Wetlands Carbon 
Assessment. The expected outcomes of the initiative include the safeguarding and enhancing 
biological diversity, carbon sequestration and ground water recharge being co benefit.

centres of excellence for talented athletes in Bihar, particularly in the 
Seemanchal region; and 
 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
 
ANSWER 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS & SPORTS  
[ DR. MANSUKH MANDAVIYA ] 

Page 2 of 2 
 
(a) to (f) ‘Sports’ being a State subject, the responsibility for 
development of sports, including reviewing of ongoing programmes 
implemented for talent identification, training of athletes, sports science 
and sports medi cine support and the effective utilization of sports 
infrastructure, rests primarily with the respective State/Union Territory 
Governments. The Union Government supplements their efforts by 
bridging critical gaps through its schemes and programmes. The Khelo 
India Scheme is being implemented across the country, including in the 
State of Bihar, with the objective of strengthening sports infrastructure, 
identifying and nurturing sporting talent and providing structured 
training and other support to athletes. Under the Scheme, financial 
assistance is provided for development of sports infrastructure and 
support is extended through Khelo India State Centres of Excellence 
(KISCEs), Khelo India Centres (KICs), Khelo India Accredited Academies 
(KIAAs), Khelo India Athletes (KIAs) and other components of the 
Scheme. 
 
The Khelo India Scheme is a demand -driven scheme. Proposals received 
from State/UT Governments and other eligible entities are considered for 
financial support, subject to their completeness, technical f easibility, 
infrastructure gaps, sporting potential, readiness for implementation and 
availability of funds under the Scheme.  
 
The details of various sports facilities under the Khelo India Scheme, 
such as Sports Infrastructure, Khelo India Centres (KICs), Khelo India 
State Centres of Excellence (KISCEs) and Khelo India Accredited 
Academies (KIAAs) along with Khelo India Athletes (KIAs) and coaches, 
across the country, including in Seemanchal region of the State of Bihar, 
are available in the public domain  on the dashboard of the Ministry at 
https://dashboard.kheloindia.gov.in. 
 
The implementation of the Khelo India Scheme is continuously 
monitored through established review and monitoring mechanisms and 
regular interaction with State Governments, implementing agencies and 
other stakeholders. The Government has taken various measures to 
strengthen talent identification and development, including identification 
of sporting talent through Khelo India competitions and Talent 
Identification and Development initi atives, provision of structured 
training through Khelo India Centres, Khelo India State Centres of 
Excellence and Khelo India Accredited Academies, and support for 
coaching, sports science, sports medicine, nutrition and competition 
exposure, as per the extant Scheme guidelines.

entries.t: Gyan Bharatam Mission and Preservation of Manuscript Heritage
entries.head:
GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
MINISTRY OF CULTURE 
LOK SABHA 
UNSTARRED QUESTION NO. 2307 
TO BE ANSWERED ON 03.08.2026 
 
Gyan Bharatam Mission and Preservation of Manuscript Heritage 
 
2307. Smt. Himadri Singh: 
          Shri Bhartruhari Mahtab: 
          Smt. Shobhanaben Mahendrasinh Baraiya:  
          Shri Tanuj Punia:  
          Shri Manish Jaiswal: 
          Shri Satish Kumar Gautam:  
          Smt. Mala Rajya Laxmi Shah:  
          Shri Gopal Jee Thakur: 
          Shri Alok Sharma: 
          Shri Janardan Mishra:  
          Shri Jagdambika Pal: 
 
Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of main objective of the recently launched 'Gyan Bharatam Mission' along with funds 
allocated by the Government thereon; 
(b) the details of number of manuscripts and rare texts identified, documented and digitised under 
the said Mission, State/UT-wise, particularly in Bihar especially in Darbhanga region and 
district-wise in Madhya Pradesh, since its launch; 
(c) whether the Government has established any institutional mechanism to encourage participation 
of private custodians, religious institutions, libraries and universities in the preservation and 
digitisation of manuscripts; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) the details of measures taken/being taken by the Government to promote scholarly access, 
research and public outreach of digitised manuscripts under the said Mission; and 
(f) whether the Government is considering for taking any special initiative to preserve Darbhanga's 
rich Mithila manuscript tradition, Sanskrit texts and historical documents? 
 
ANSWER 
 
MINISTER OF CULTURE AND TOURISM 
(SHRI GAJENDRA SINGH SHEKHAWAT) 
 
(a) & (b) Gyan Bharatam Mission (GBM), announced during Union Budget 2025-26, is an initiative of 
the Ministry of Culture (MoC), Government of India to undertake manuscripts related activities. The 
objectives of this initiative are as follows: 
I. To leverage advanced technology to significantly enhance the pace of digitization and 
documentation of manuscripts. 

II. Conducting survey and registration of manuscripts. 
III. To document and catalogue Indian manuscripts, wherever they may be, maintain accurate and 
up-to-date information about them and the conditions under which they may be conserved. 
IV. To facilitate usage of manuscripts and promote ready access to these manuscripts through 
publications, both in book form as well as machine readable form. 
V. To facilitate conservation and preservation of manuscripts through training awareness and 
financial support. 
VI. To boost scholarship and research in the study of Indian languages and manuscriptology. 
VII. To build up a National Digital Repository (NDR). 
 
To support the initiative, the Standing Finance Committee (SFC) has sanctioned Rs.491.66 crore for 
the period 2025-2031. National Manuscript Survey was launched in March, 2026 across all States and 
Union Territories (UTs) of the country to identify and document manuscript holdings, repositories and 
custodians representing diverse languages and scripts. During the survey, more than 1.19 crore 
manuscripts have been reported. The total number of digitized manuscripts available across the country 
is over 8 lakh, out of which, more than 4.40 lakh manuscripts are available on Gyan Bharatam portal at 
present for public access, in view mode which is accessible state-wise. 
 
(c) & (d)   The mission has established an institutional mechanism through Cluster Centres and 
Independent Centres which include universities, research institutions, libraries, archives, private 
custodians, religious institutions, and other stakeholders to undertake manuscript related activities. 
States / Union Territories (UTs) have also been engaged to act as Nodal Coordinating Authority for 
Gyan Bharatam implementation within the State / UT concerned. 
 
(e) Access to digitized copies of manuscript is facilitated in accordance with the rights of 
custodians and rights holders. Wherever permissible, manuscripts and associated metadata may be 
made available for public and scholarly research through the National Digital Repository, while 
sensitive, restricted or rights-protected materials may be subject to appropriate access conditions. 
 
(f)  GBM is a pan-India initiative aimed at preserving India’s manuscript heritage, irrespective of 
script, language, knowledge tradition, region, or the custodial traditions of communities. Institutions 
located in Bihar namely (i) Nava Nalanda Mahavihar, Nalanda (ii) Khuda Bakhsh Oriental Public 
Library, Patna and (iii) Shri Bodh Gaya Math, Bodh Gaya have onboarded with GBM to undertake 
manuscript related activities.
